study.title: Exercise may help mental health, QoL and pain in osteoporosis
study.evidence_note: Based on 23 RCTs, with pooled effects and GRADE reported in the review.
study.confidence_note: Full text reported the methods, pooled results, subgroup analyses and GRADE tables.
study.impact_line: Exercise is reasonable to recommend for symptoms, but the best dose and mode are still unclear.
summary: Exercise improved mental health, QoL and pain in pooled analyses.
Heterogeneity was high for the main outcomes.
Clinical Pilates and resistance-based programmes often looked best in subgroups.
Pain benefit was small on the pooled SMD scale.

pico.c: Treatment as usual, no intervention, or unsupervised activity advice
pico.o: Mental health, quality of life, pain and physical function

limits: Mostly older women; findings may not transfer well to men.
Exercise content, intensity and progression were inconsistently reported.
Heterogeneity was substantial or considerable for several pooled outcomes.
Some subgroup effects came from small numbers of studies.
One study had self-reported osteoporosis and was sensitivity-tested out.
study.bottom_line: Exercise probably helps mental health, quality of life and pain in osteoporosis, but the pooled effects are heterogeneous and the best exercise recipe is still uncertain.

methods.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
methods.setting: Six databases searched; studies from multiple countries
methods.participants: Adults with clinically diagnosed osteoporosis; 2120 participants across 23 studies
methods.intervention: Exercise or physical activity programmes of varied type, dose and supervision
methods.comparator: Treatment as usual, no intervention, or unsupervised physical activity advice
methods.primary_outcome: Mental health, quality of life and pain

results.detail: 20 RCTs, 1676 participants. Heterogeneity was considerable: I2 = 85%, p < 0.00001. GRADE was moderate.
12 RCTs, 1130 participants. Heterogeneity was considerable: I2 = 84%, p < 0.00001. GRADE was moderate.
16 RCTs, 1452 participants. Heterogeneity was substantial: I2 = 63%, p = 0.0004. GRADE was low.
4 RCTs, 229 participants. Heterogeneity was substantial: I2 = 63%, p = 0.02. GRADE was moderate, downgraded for imprecision.

how_to_apply: Progressive resistance and balance work were the most consistent elements.
Three sessions per week often looked best in subgroup analyses.
Do not over-interpret subgroup results from small study sets.
Expect benefit on symptoms, not guaranteed bone outcomes.
Pilates may help, but the evidence base was small.
not_for: Very frail patients excluded from trials
Claims about bone density change from this review

strengths: Sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses were reported
weaknesses: Clinical significance thresholds were not uniform
Some subgroup findings rested on small studies
appraisal.funding_conflicts: Open Access funding via CAUL member institutions; philanthropic grant and PhD scholarship. Authors reported no conflicts of interest.

domains.support: P86: exclusions listed; one paper not retrieved

domains.reason: Sensitivity analyses removed high-risk studies and discussion linked findings to study quality.
Funnel plots were inspected for primary outcomes.
domains.support: P64-P75: funnel plots and publication bias

grade.reason: Most trials were low risk or had some concerns; four mental-health studies were high risk for statistical conclusion validity.
Mental health heterogeneity was considerable: I2 = 85%, p < 0.00001.
Adults with osteoporosis, exercise comparators and patient-important outcomes matched the review question.
Pooled mental-health estimate was statistically significant with 1676 participants across 20 RCTs.
Funnel plots were inspected; publication bias was not flagged for mental health.

clinical_significance: Mental health and QoL improved, but the paper does not give an MCID for the SMDs, so clinical importance is uncertain.
Pain SMD looks small; the review itself calls the clinical meaning variable.
For QUALEFFO-41 pain, the change may be clinically relevant.
For VAS pain at rest, the change may or may not be meaningful.
comparator_fairness: Comparators were credible overall: usual care, no intervention, or unsupervised advice.
Dose and contact time were often lower than the active programmes, so expectation control was limited.
This is not a sham-controlled exercise trial.
alternative_explanations: Natural history may explain part of the change in a chronic condition.
Regression to the mean is plausible, especially in small studies.
Non-specific attention and group contact may have contributed.
Co-interventions and differential attrition could have influenced some trials.
spin: The abstract and conclusion broadly match the pooled results.
The paper emphasises favourable subgroups despite high heterogeneity and small subgroup sizes.
Some subgroup language is stronger than the data support.
fit_with_evidence: The review is broadly consistent with prior systematic reviews cited by the authors and with exercise guidance for osteoporosis.
It extends the evidence by pooling mental health and pain outcomes together, but does not settle the optimal prescription.
external_validity: ✓ Mostly older adults with osteoporosis, similar to many outpatient caseloads
✓ Supervised clinic/gym and home programmes both featured
✗ 95.1% female, so male transfer is limited
✗ Many studies excluded severe comorbidity; real-world caseloads are messier
would_change_my_mind: A large, well-reported RCT showing no symptom benefit despite low attrition and prespecified MCIDs would weaken this conclusion.
A consistent effect in men, frailer adults, or higher-quality trials would strengthen it.

study.patient_explanation: Exercise seems to help pain, mood and daily function in people with osteoporosis. The best programme is not settled, but supervised, progressive exercise is a reasonable option.
open_questions: Does benefit differ by fracture history or sex?
Which outcome measure best captures mental health in osteoporosis?
key_findings: Exercise improved mental health, QoL and pain in pooled analyses.
Heterogeneity was high, so average effects are uncertain.
Clinical Pilates and resistance-based programmes often looked best in subgroups.
Pain benefit was small on the pooled SMD scale.
